To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
electrospray ionisation and FTICR MS can be used to study non-covalent protein-ligand and non-covalent interactions in solution phase.

the gas-phase dissociation of electrospray ions is a useful tool for studying protein-ligand interactions, and for studying protein-protein interactions, and that the gas-phase results can be interpreted in the context of solution-phase results.

the binding constants of non-covalent complexes of proteins can be determined from the relative abundance of the isotopomers in the gas phase and that the binding constants so determined are in good agreement with those measured independently in solution.
In summary, our research is concerned with
using electrospray MS to investigate protein-ligand and -protein interactions.
the application of electrospray ionisation to the study of protein-protein and protein-ligand interactions, with the aim of providing new insights into the structure and energetics of such complexes.
the application of electrospray ionisation and MS to the study of protein complexes, and in particular with the elucidation of the nature of non-covalent interactions in solution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the technique is a powerful one for the study of protein-ligand interactions and for the characterization of protein-protein complexes.

electrospray MS is an extremely useful technique, and the only one currently available, for the characterization of protein-ligand and -protein interactions, but that it should be used in combination with other techniques, and not as a replacement for any of them.
electrospray and FTICR MS is the method of choice for characterizing non-covalent protein-ligand and non-covalent homo- and hetero-oligomeric complexes of proteins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

electrospray ionisation and mass spectrometric techniques can be used to determine the stoichiometry of non-covalent complexes, to determine the binding constants of complexes in solution and to determine the relative affinities of ligands for a binding site.
the approach can be used with great success for complexes of proteins up to 30 kDa, but that the approach is less successful for complexes of proteins of higher mass.
the technique is a powerful one, but it is not a panacea for protein-ligand interactions, and its limitations should be appreciated.
The main takeaway from our work is that

electrospray and FTICR MS can be used to determine the stoichiometry, binding constants and structures of protein-ligand and of protein-protein complexes in solution, with the added bonus of being able to measure the binding constants of these complexes in the gas phase.
the technique is a useful adjunct to the study of protein interactions, but it is not a substitute for more traditional techniques.
electrospray and FTICR MS are a very powerful combination for studying protein-ligand and -protein interactions.
